I'm a 53-year-old woman who's been farming these fields in Quzhou for over thirty years. My family has about 10 mu of good flat land on the North China Plain, and I know what this soil can do. I've only got primary schooling, but I know my land better than any book.

This year, like most years, I'll stick to the wheat-maize rotation. That's what works here. In the autumn I'll sow winter wheat — probably an improved variety like Luyuan 502 or Jimai 22, the kind you buy from the seed dealer in town. Before sowing I'll run the rotary tiller to break up the stubble and smooth the field. I put down about 100 jin of compound fertilizer per mu as basal dressing — the special formula kind, around 18-22-5 — and then sow the wheat. The wheat needs water, so I'll irrigate four times: once in winter to protect against the cold, and then a few times in spring when the wheat is jointing and filling. In spring I'll also topdress with some ammonium bicarbonate when the wheat starts turning green — about 50 jin per mu. I'll spray insecticide twice, herbicide once, and fungicide once when I see the diseases starting. If the weather cooperates, I expect about 1000 jin per mu.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I don't have much time before the rains come, so I plant summer maize right away — no-tillage, straight into the wheat stubble. I'll use hybrid seed, Denghai 605 most likely. It gives good yield and the dealers always have it. Basal dressing is about 80 jin per mu of compound fertilizer, the high-nitrogen kind for corn. Maize doesn't need as much water as wheat — two irrigations is usually enough, one when it's small and one during tasseling. I'll spray insecticide twice and herbicide once. If things go well, I can get about 1100 jin per mu.

I don't grow cotton or those specialty crops like some people do — too much labor, too much risk, and who has time to prune cotton all day? Wheat and maize feed my family, and I can sell the surplus. The grain prices might not be high, but they're steady. I don't gamble with new-fangled methods; I do what my neighbors do and what has put food on the table for decades.
